findings.section: Q2. Single-threaded performance cost, per version
findings.quote: Microbenchmarks from the release week are consistent with the official range.
findings.problem: Source 013 (cited as [10]) is on disk and reports the opposite for 3.14.0: its single-process, single-threaded Mandelbrot script ran 33% longer on the free-threaded build and the multiprocessing variant 43% longer, far outside the 5-10% official range; the draft names the study but withholds the number.
findings.fix: Microbenchmarks from the release week are not uniformly consistent with the official range. One Mandelbrot study on Astral's Clang-built 3.14.0 interpreters found the single-process, single-threaded script ran 33% longer on the free-threaded build and the multiprocessing variant 43% longer, while the threaded variant ran about 47.7% faster than the GIL-build baseline; the author recommends benchmarking your own workload before choosing a concurrency approach [10].

findings.section: Q2. Single-threaded performance cost, per version
findings.quote: Other independent runs exist in the corpus but their numbers were not extracted here: a pure-Python fibonacci and bubble-sort matrix across interpreter versions, whose author warns
findings.problem: The numbers are on disk: source 011 gives 3.14 FT at 91% of the standard interpreter's single-threaded speed (0.91x) with 3.1x / ~2x multi-threaded gains and a do-not-recommend verdict for non-GIL-bound workloads; declining to extract them weakens the per-version answer to Q2.
findings.fix: Two other independent runs put numbers on the same question. A pure-Python Fibonacci and bubble-sort matrix across interpreter versions measured 3.14's free-threaded interpreter at 91% of the standard interpreter's speed on single-threaded Fibonacci, against roughly 3.1x faster on four-thread Fibonacci and about 2x on four-thread bubble sort; its author does not recommend the free-threaded build for code not directly slowed by the GIL and warns

findings.section: Q2. Single-threaded performance cost, per version
findings.quote: The cost that the headline percentage hides is memory.
findings.problem: PEP 779 (source 002, already cited as [2]) quantifies the memory cost at about 15-20% higher use (geometric mean, pyperformance) and sets a 20% Phase II target; the draft calls memory "less advertised" and gives no number although one is on disk in a primary source.
findings.fix: The cost that the headline percentage hides is memory. PEP 779 put a number on it at acceptance time: free-threaded Python showed about 15-20% higher memory use (geometric mean, as measured by pyperformance), the PEP proposed 20% as the Phase II target, and its authors said higher memory use is realistically the price of efficient, safe free threading [2].

findings.section: Q3. Library compatibility: NumPy, pandas, Django
findings.quote: Verdict: NumPy is compatible; correctness of shared mutable arrays is the user's responsibility, as it always was.
findings.problem: The NumPy v2.5 manual (source 007, cited as [13] for thread-safety advice) states that free-threaded support, new in 2.1, is "experimental", and that dtype=np.object_ arrays are no longer GIL-protected, creating data races impossible outside free-threaded Python; both caveats from the cited source are absent from the verdict.
findings.fix: Verdict: NumPy is compatible, although its own v2.5 manual still describes free-threaded support (new in NumPy 2.1 with CPython 3.13) as experimental; correctness of shared mutable arrays is the user's responsibility, as it always was, and arrays with dtype=np.object_ carry a new class of data race because their Python-object elements are no longer protected by the GIL [13].

findings.section: Q3. Library compatibility: NumPy, pandas, Django
findings.quote: and test the Cython extension modules [14].
findings.problem: The pandas tracking issue (source 009) also records that the C extension modules were marked with the Py_mod_gil slot (#59135) and Cython's free-threading directive was enabled globally (#59248) with green CI; this bears directly on the open question of whether pandas itself re-enables the GIL and is omitted.
findings.fix: and test the Cython extension modules [14]. The same issue records the C extension modules being marked with the Py_mod_gil slot (#59135), the Cython free-threading directive enabled globally (#59248), and green CI with Cython nightly [14]; since the automatic GIL re-enable is triggered by importing an extension not marked as supporting free threading [5], those markings weigh against pandas' own modules being the trigger for the partial re-enable reported in the April 2026 survey.

findings.section: Q3. Library compatibility: NumPy, pandas, Django
findings.quote: Verdict: Django runs and its suite passes under 3.14t as of mid-2026, but it has no formal support declaration and its per-request scaling on free-threaded builds is still being fixed.
findings.problem: Source 014 says only that the suite "can now run" under free-threading after asgiref 3.12 and test tweaks, names no interpreter version, and the same post expects "more thread related issues"; "passes under 3.14t" is not in the note.
findings.fix: Verdict: Django runs, and as of July 2026 its test suite can be run under free-threading (after asgiref 3.12 and some test tweaks), with the reporter expecting more thread-related issues to surface; it has no formal support declaration and its per-request scaling on free-threaded builds is still being fixed [7].

findings.quote: Django is pure Python, so it is not on the tracker and "works" in the trivial sense; the questions are thread safety of its internals and dependencies, and scaling.
findings.problem: Uncited assertion; the tracker's pure-Python scope statement [6] and Wouters' remark that regular Python code needs little or nothing but existing threading bugs become more likely [3] are on disk and support it.
findings.fix: Django is pure Python, so it is not on the tracker and "works" in the trivial sense [6]; Wouters' caveat for pure-Python code is that nothing needs changing unless the code already has multi-threading bugs, which the free-threaded build makes more likely to surface [3]. The questions are thread safety of its internals and dependencies, and scaling.

findings.section: Q1. Which CPython versions support the free-threaded build, and with what status
findings.quote: No specific version has been committed to for making free-threading the default; the timeline depends on library adoption [4].
findings.problem: The primary source on disk (PEP 779) says the Phase III decision is left for a future PEP and will revolve around community support, willingness, and clear benefit; the draft supports this point with a blog only.
findings.fix: No specific version has been committed to for making free-threading the default; the timeline depends on library adoption [4]. PEP 779 itself leaves the Phase III decision to a future PEP and expects it to revolve around community support, willingness, and demonstrated benefit [2].

findings.section: Open questions
findings.quote: Python 3.14.5 reverted the default build's incremental GC to the 3.13 generational GC after production memory-pressure reports; whether the free-threaded build's separate collector was affected is not stated in the corpus.
findings.problem: Factual assertion without a citation; the revert is documented in the 3.14 What's New (source 008) and the separate free-threaded collector in source 003.
findings.fix: Python 3.14.5 reverted the default build's incremental GC to the 3.13 generational GC after production memory-pressure reports [1]; whether the free-threaded build's separate collector [3] was affected is not stated in the corpus.
